Renaissance Art. The visual and sculptural revolution that accompanied the Renaissance revival of classical learning, spanning roughly 1300 to 1600 and originating in Italy. Artists rediscovered techniques lost since antiquity—linear perspective, anatomical precision, naturalism—and reintegrated them with Christian theology to create new possibilities for representation.

The Renaissance began in Florence as artists studied Roman ruins and recovered classical proportional systems and sculptural ideals. Filippo Brunelleschi invented linear perspective, which enabled convincing spatial depth and allowed artists to depict three dimensions on flat surfaces. The movement emphasized anatomical accuracy achieved through life drawing and often cadaver dissection, with human bodies becoming the primary subject.

Renaissance art introduced secular and humanistic subjects alongside religious themes: classical mythology, portraiture, landscapes, still life. Sculpture was pioneered by Donatello and Ghiberti, who recovered Roman contrapposto stance and naturalism in bronze and marble. Painting advanced through systematic use of oil paint; layered glazes and luminous color replaced tempera's flatness.

The High Renaissance, spanning from 1495 to 1520, represented the apex. Masters like Michelangelo, Raphael, and Leonardo da Vinci perfected the vocabulary. Renaissance artists were often polymaths: painters trained in architecture, studied anatomy, conducted scientific observations, embodying the era's integrated intellectual ambition.

The movement gradually spread north to the Low Countries, France, and Germany, adapting local traditions to Italian principles of naturalism and classical reference. Renaissance art established the standards for Western artistic training for centuries: life drawing, anatomy, perspective, and classical ideals became the curriculum.
